subject: Computer Networking
title: Monitoring and Alerting
description: Learn Monitoring and Alerting in one minute.

hook.text: A server fails at 3 AM and no one is watching. How long until someone notices? Monitoring closes that gap.

buildup.text: Tools track metrics: latency, error rates, CPU, memory. Dashboards show the system's health at a glance.

discovery.text: Alert rules notify on-call engineers when thresholds are crossed. PagerDuty wakes people up when it matters.

twist.text: Too many alerts cause fatigue. Engineers start ignoring them. The real emergency gets buried in noise.

climax.text: Good monitoring answers: is it broken, where, and why? The third question is always the hardest.

punchline.text: You can't fix what you can't see. Monitor what matters.

quiz.question: What is alert fatigue?
options: When too many alerts cause engineers to ignore them
When monitoring tools crash from overuse
When alerts are sent too slowly to be useful

details.summary: Effective monitoring and alerting systems detect outages before users do and provide the data needed for rapid diagnosis. The best monitoring covers infrastructure health, application performance, and business metrics.
details.whyItMatters: You cannot fix what you cannot see. Monitoring is the difference between detecting a problem in seconds and discovering it hours later from angry customers.
takeaways: Monitor infrastructure, application, and business metrics
Alert on symptoms like error rates, not just causes like CPU
Dashboards should answer why is it broken within seconds

faq.question: What should network monitoring systems track?
faq.answer: Track latency, packet loss, bandwidth utilization, error rates, and connection counts at minimum. Application-level metrics like response time and error codes reveal problems invisible to network-level monitoring. Business metrics like transactions per second detect customer-facing impact.

faq.question: What makes alerting effective versus noisy?
faq.answer: Effective alerts fire on conditions that require human action. Noisy alerts fire on transient conditions that resolve themselves, causing alert fatigue. Good alerting uses thresholds, time windows, and anomaly detection to reduce false positives while catching real incidents.
